newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's agent warns loss-making spiral looms.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's agent warns loss-making spiral looms.

text.p: Lloyds of London faces the return of the so-called spiral which was at the centre of the insurance market's problems in the 1980s, members' agent Christie Brockbank Shipton Ltd said in its latest newsletter.

"With rates falling, too much capacity and worrying signs of a developing spiral market, there are parallels with the late 1980s as more capital piles in regardless," Charles Harbord-Hammond, managing director of CBSL, said.

An insurance spiral occurs when insurance syndicates or companies reinsure risks or part of risks they have already insured. This runs counter to the basic premise of reinsurance -- to spread rather than concentrate risk.
It also reduces the amount of premium income available to pay any claims as more of the premium is taken out in brokerage and other fees.
Concentration of risk in this way caused massive losses for the Gooda Walker and Feltrim syndicates at Lloyd's in the wake of the Piper Alpha oil rig disaster.

"There is no doubt that mini-spirals are beginning to be built up. As pressure on income increases through 1997, business will increasingly be written on the back of reinsurance programmes with less and less exclusions," CBSL said.
New Lloyd's capital will be particularly at risk of repeating the errors of the 1980s, it said, adding that too much capital had been committed for 1997.
With insurance rates currently in a cyclical decline, profit forecasts being quoted by some Lloyd's insurers are unrealistic.
"Such margins are only achievable for a short period in any cycle and that period has now passed," the members' agent said.
Harbord-Hammond said he was also concerned about an obligation on the market to use at least 80 percent of its available capacity to underwrite in 1997.
"It cannot be wise for Lloyd's to be tied to using 80 percent of its capacity in a softer market, when it failed to do so in a harder one."
